title: Dakgalbi
subtitle: Spicy stir-fried chicken with rice cakes and cabbage
excerpt: A fiery, satisfying stir-fry of chicken, chewy rice cakes, and cabbage tossed in a bold gochujang sauce. It is a street-food staple from Chuncheon that takes about 35 minutes and serves 4. Everything cooks in one pan over high heat.
sourceNotes: Dakgalbi originated in Chuncheon, a city in Gangwon Province in the 1960s. It was originally cooked over charcoal in round, dome-shaped pans. The dish spread rapidly across South Korea and became one of the most recognisable regional specialities in the country, with Chuncheon now famous for its dakgalbi restaurant street.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The chicken can be marinated in the sauce for up to 4 hours in the fridge before cooking.

glossaryTerms.definition: Gochujang is a fermented Korean chilli paste made from red chilli powder, glutinous rice, fermented soybean powder, and salt. It has a complex, deeply savoury heat with a slight sweetness from the fermented rice. It is one of the cornerstone condiments of Korean cooking and forms the base of marinades, sauces, and soups.

Tteok is the Korean word for rice cakes made from pounded or ground rice flour. There are hundreds of varieties, from sweet filled cakes to the cylindrical garae-tteok used in stir-fries and tteokbokki. When cooked in a sauce, they become chewy and sticky, absorbing the surrounding flavours while maintaining their characteristic texture.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and is ready in about 35 minutes including marinating. Dakgalbi is a bold, high-heat stir-fry built on chicken thighs, chewy cylindrical rice cakes called

. Everything goes into one wide pan over high heat for a fast, smoky finish.

Soak the rice cakes in cold water for 20 minutes before cooking if they have been refrigerated or dried out. This softens them so they cook evenly without hardening on the outside. Do not crowd the pan: use the widest pan you have or cook in two batches. The sauce should sizzle and caramelise, not steam.

content.text: Mix together the gochujang, gochugaru, soy sauce, garlic, sugar, and mirin in a large bowl to make the marinade.
Add the chicken pieces and toss to coat. Leave to marinate for at least 10 minutes while you prep the vegetables. Longer marinating (up to 4 hours in the fridge) deepens the flavour.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan or wok over high heat until smoking.
Add the chicken and cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until coloured on the outside.
Add the drained rice cakes and cabbage. Stir-fry for 5 to 6 minutes until the cabbage is wilted and the rice cakes are heated through and slightly charred at the edges.
Add the spring onions and toss for 1 minute. If the pan looks dry, add a splash of water to loosen the sauce.
Check the chicken is cooked through, then drizzle with sesame oil and serve immediately with steamed rice.

items.symptom: The rice cakes are hard in the centre
items.cause: They were not soaked before cooking or were cooked too briefly
items.fix: Soak refrigerated rice cakes in cold water for at least 20 minutes. If still firm in the pan, add 3 tablespoons of water, cover for 2 minutes, then uncover and stir

items.symptom: The sauce burns before the chicken cooks through
items.cause: The heat was too high or the pan too small, causing the sauce to caramelise too fast
items.fix: Add a splash of water to the pan and reduce the heat slightly. Stir continuously to prevent sticking

items.cause: Boneless chicken thighs can tighten up if the heat is very high
items.fix: Cut pieces larger, around 4cm, and cook over medium-high rather than maximum heat. The sauce should provide enough moisture to keep things tender

content.text: Dakgalbi comes from Chuncheon, a city about 80 kilometres east of Seoul. The dish became a student favourite in the 1970s and 1980s because it was filling and cheap. Today Chuncheon has an entire street lined with dakgalbi restaurants where the dish is cooked at the table on round flat griddles. Visitors travel specifically to eat it there. At home, it is a quick, satisfying weeknight meal that comes together in one pan with minimal fuss.
